**Abstract**

India's Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), the official national labor force survey, shows the worker-population ratio of women aged 15 and over rising from `r f(w("wpr", "y17"))` percent in 2017--18 to `r f(w("wpr", "y23"))` percent in 2023--24, a near doubling under unchanged definitions of work, though field instructions were revised. Using unit-level data from the two nationally representative survey rounds (`r f0(nwom(2017))` and `r f0(nwom(2023))` women aged 15 and over), I reproduce the published estimates and decompose the rise with exact additive accounting, design-based standard errors, and a Kitagawa shift-share decomposition. Consistent with earlier studies, own-account work and unpaid help account for `r f0(selfsh)` percent of the `r f(dW)`-point rise and agriculture for `r sh(w("ag"), dW)` percent. The new results concern measurement. Women whose principal activity was outside the labor force, mostly domestic duties, and who were counted as workers only through a subsidiary activity account for `r f(shs("share"))` percent (SE `r f(shs("se"))`) of the full-period rise, building on year-by-year splits by Kar and Mohanan. Weekly hours worked per woman rose by `r hrsg` percent, against `r wprg` percent for the worker-population ratio. In 2023--24, `r f0(et("Women", 1) + et("Women", 2))` percent of self-employed women in primary production produced only or mainly for household consumption; excluding such output, the rule closest to the 2013 international definition of employment, puts the usual-status ratio at `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x12"))` percent. The rise is concentrated in the forms of work that are most sensitive to how surveys probe. For India, and for other countries adopting the 2013 standards, headline employment rates are best read alongside principal-status, hours-based, and own-use-adjusted measures.

**Keywords:** women's employment; measurement of work; unpaid family workers; own-use production; labor force surveys; India

# Introduction

Between 2017--18 and 2023--24, India's official labor force survey recorded a near doubling of women's employment. The worker-population ratio (WPR) of women aged 15 and over in usual status rose from `r f(w("wpr", "y17"))` to `r f(w("wpr", "y23"))` percent, and the published series rose in every year in between [@nso2024pn]. The definitions of work did not change. Earlier studies have shown that the rise lies in rural self-employment in agriculture [@ara2025], and the unit-level data confirm it: own-account work and unpaid help in household enterprises account for `r f0(selfsh)` percent of the `r f(dW)`-point rise and agriculture for `r sh(w("ag"), dW)` percent. Unit-level work has also split the rise into principal and subsidiary components year by year and bounded the effect of the revised field instructions [@kar2025; @thakur2025if]. This paper adds four things. First, it puts a design-based standard error on the share of the full-period rise that lies at the margin of what counts as work: women whose principal activity was outside the labor force, mostly domestic duties, and who were counted as workers only through a subsidiary economic activity account for `r f(shs("share"))` percent of the rise (SE `r f(shs("se"))`; 95 percent confidence interval `r f(shs("lo"))` to `r f(shs("hi"))`; Table 2). Second, it compares persons with hours: mean weekly hours of work per woman rose by `r hrsg` percent, about half the `r wprg`-percent rise in the WPR. Third, it estimates an own-use-adjusted rate: in 2023--24, `r f0(et("Women", 1) + et("Women", 2))` percent of self-employed women in primary production produced only or mainly for the household's own consumption, work that the 2013 international standard classifies as own-use production rather than employment [@ilo2013]; excluding it lowers the women's WPR to `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x12"))` percent (Table 5). Fourth, a shift-share decomposition tests whether changes in composition explain the rise (Table 6).

These results matter beyond India for two reasons. First, many countries are revising their labor force surveys to implement the 2013 resolution of the International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS), which separates employment (work for pay or profit) from own-use production work. Survey experiments in Tanzania, Ghana and the countries of the International Labour Organization (ILO) pilot program show that measured women's employment depends on how questions are asked and how carefully enumerators probe for agricultural and household-based activity [@bardasi2011; @gaddis2021; @benes2018]. Those studies vary the questionnaire within a single survey. India's recent experience is a national-scale case of the same sensitivity outside an experiment: a headline rate that moved by `r f(dW)` points under formally unchanged definitions, with the change concentrated in exactly the categories that the experimental literature identifies as most sensitive to probing. Second, women's employment rates are widely used as indicators of progress and as targets in national and international policy. If a large part of a measured rise is subsidiary and own-use work, the headline rate alone can overstate changes in women's paid work, earnings and economic independence, and the measures needed to interpret it have to be published alongside it.

The rise also bears on population policy, because women's employment is treated as a demographic variable as well as an economic one. Projections of the labor force, assessments of a demographic dividend, and discussions of fertility, age at marriage, schooling and the care of children and older persons all use women's employment as an input or as a pathway. These uses assume that a higher recorded rate means a change in how women allocate time between market work, household production and care. If the recorded rise lies mainly in work that sits beside domestic duties, then extrapolating the rate into future labor supply, or reading it as evidence of a changed bargaining position within households, may overstate what has changed. The earlier literature on the decline in participation linked women's work to household income, education and social norms [@klasen2015; @jayachandran2021]. The links between employment and those outcomes are unlikely to be the same for every form of work. A rate that mixes wage work, unpaid family help and subsidiary activity cannot support a single demographic reading. This is a reason to publish the components of the rate along with the rate, and it is a point about interpretation, not a criticism of the survey.

A rise of this size has prompted a debate about its meaning. Studies using published tables and unit-level data show that it is concentrated among rural women and in self-employment, and that earnings from self-employment did not keep pace [@apu2023; @ara2025; @thakur2025]. One interpretation is that it reflects distress, with women entering low-productivity family work as household incomes came under pressure [@apu2023; @jha2026]. Another is that additional family labor in agriculture is productive and therefore a positive development [@goldar2026]. A third is that part of the rise reflects how completely women's existing activity is recorded as work. @thakur2025 argue that revised instructions in the 2023--24 survey contributed to moving women from outside the labor force into self-employment. Women's work in rural India is often part-time, seasonal, home-based and close to the line between production for the market, production for the household's own use and domestic work, and surveys are known to be sensitive to how such work is probed [@beneria1981; @langsten2008; @bardasi2011; @hirway2011; @deshpande2024].

This paper does not try to choose between these interpretations directly. Instead, it provides the accounting that any interpretation needs. As groundwork, it reproduces `r nexact` of `r nval` published headline estimates from the unit-level data, decomposes the change in the women's WPR exactly by status in employment, by industry and by capacity, and sets the dates of the published changes in field instructions against the annual series; the principal and subsidiary split and the timing evidence build on @kar2025. On this groundwork it adds the four elements listed above: a design-based standard error for the share of the full-period rise that comes from subsidiary-only work; a comparison of the rise in persons with the rise in hours of work per woman, a measure that does not depend on where the line between workers and non-workers is drawn; an own-use-adjusted WPR, estimated from a question on the destination of output that was introduced in the 2023--24 survey and consistent with the 2013 international definition of employment; and a shift-share decomposition that tests whether changes in population composition account for the rise.

Five findings stand out. The first confirms earlier work [@ara2025]; the other four correspond to the four elements above. First, own-account work and unpaid help in household enterprises account for `r f0(selfsh)` percent of the rise and regular wage employment for `r sh(w("s_reg"), dW)` percent, and `r sh(w("ag"), dW)` percent of the rise is in agriculture. Second, building on year-by-year splits of the workforce into principal and subsidiary components [@kar2025], I estimate that `r f(shs("share"))` percent (SE `r f(shs("se"))`) of the full-period rise consists of women whose principal activity is outside the labor force, mostly domestic duties, and who are counted as workers because of a subsidiary economic activity of at least 30 days in the year; women in the two domestic-duties codes alone account for `r f0(ddsh)` percent. Third, the rise is much smaller when measured in hours: the mean weekly hours worked per woman in the population rose by `r hrsg` percent, against `r wprg` percent for the WPR, and the share of women workers who worked fewer than 20 hours in the reference week rose from `r f(iw(2017, "all:Total", "lt20"))` to `r f(iw(2023, "all:Total", "lt20"))` percent. Fourth, in 2023--24, `r f0(et("Women", 1) + et("Women", 2))` percent of self-employed women in primary production reported that their output was only or mainly for the household's own consumption; excluding such work, the rule closest to the 2013 international standard, lowers the 2023--24 WPR of women from `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr"))` to `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x12"))` percent, and excluding only output used solely by the household gives an upper bound of `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x1"))` percent; both remain usual-status measures. Fifth, changes in age, education, marital status, sector and state composition do not explain the rise; it occurred within these groups, and it was largest among rural women aged 35 to 59, women with little schooling and Scheduled Tribe women.

As earlier commentary has noted [@thakur2025if; @kar2025], the field instructions for the 2023--24 survey contain an explicit list prompting enumerators to probe for work in kitchen gardens, orchards, household poultry and dairy and free collection, and worked examples on when such activity makes a woman engaged in domestic duties a subsidiary worker [@nso2023man]. These were not in the 2017--18 instructions [@nso2016man], and the survey's own note dates the worked examples to clarifications first provided for the 2022--23 survey [@nso2023note]. The definitions of work did not change, and the data cannot show how much the instructions contributed. The point is narrower: the categories in which the rise is concentrated are exactly those in which responses depend most on probing, so the rise should be read with that in mind.

The paper contributes to three literatures. For research on women's employment in India, which has largely studied the earlier decline [@klasen2015; @mehrotra2017; @afridi2018; @lahoti2016; @sarkar2019], it adds design-based uncertainty to the principal and subsidiary accounting of the recent reversal and separates persons from hours. For the literature on the measurement of women's work [@beneria1981; @langsten2008; @bardasi2011; @gaddis2021; @benes2018], it adds a large non-experimental case in which a large change in the measured rate is concentrated in the most measurement-sensitive categories. And for the implementation of the 2013 ICLS standards, it shows how a single destination-of-output question allows a survey that keeps the older, broader concept of work to report an employment rate consistent with the new definition. The analysis is descriptive. It does not attribute the change to any particular cause or policy.

# Background

## Women's work in India and its measurement

For more than a decade, research on women's employment in India was about decline. Successive rounds of the National Sample Survey recorded falling participation of women in the labor force between 2004--05 and 2011--12, despite rapid economic growth, falling fertility and rising education [@klasen2015; @mehrotra2017; @andres2017; @afridi2018; @chatterjee2018; @desai2019]. Explanations emphasized rising household incomes and an income effect on women's labor supply, rising enrollment in education, the shortage of jobs considered suitable for women, social norms that restrict women's mobility, and changes in the structure of agricultural work [@klasen2015; @mehrotra2017; @afridi2018; @chatterjee2018; @jayachandran2021]. The cross-country literature on a U-shaped relation between development and women's participation also predicts that women withdraw from family farm work as household incomes rise and return to the labor force later, through wage employment in services [@goldin1994; @gaddis2014; @klasen2019]. A rise in women's employment that comes mainly through self-employment in agriculture runs against both of these patterns, which is one reason the recent rise has been questioned [@ara2025; @jha2026].

Measurement has been a concern throughout. Women's work in family farms and enterprises is often not reported as work unless respondents are asked about it specifically, and the answers depend on the wording of questions, on the reference period and on who answers [@beneria1981; @langsten2008; @bardasi2011]. In India, time-use data have long recorded more economic activity by women than labor force surveys [@hirway2011], and the distinction between work for income, expenditure-saving work for the household and unpaid domestic work is important for understanding women's work [@deshpande2024]. Earlier panel evidence also shows frequent movements of Indian women into and out of work [@sarkar2019], so the measured rate depends on how intermittent work is captured.

## Recent evidence on the rise

A recent literature examines the post-2017 rise directly. @ara2025 use PLFS data to show that the rise in women's labor force participation is driven by rural women and by own-account and unpaid work in agriculture and the unorganized sector, that the share of women workers in regular salaried jobs, the organized sector and industry and services fell, and that real earnings from self-employment declined after the pandemic. @apu2023 report that women's employment rates rose after 2019 through an increase in self-employment and that real earnings from self-employment declined over the same period, and read the rise as distress-led. @jha2026 focus on the growth of unpaid family workers and argue that it reflects distress-driven employment growth. @goldar2026 question the premise that unpaid female family labor in Indian agriculture has very low productivity, which supports a more positive reading. @thakur2025 use unit-level PLFS data and argue that revised instructions in the 2023--24 survey shifted a sizable number of women from outside the labor force into self-employment, and that real incomes fell in the activities that absorbed them. In a companion article, @thakur2025if report that the number of women recorded under principal status 93 fell by about 19.8 million in 2023--24 and that the number with principal status 92 and subsidiary self-employment rose to about 8.5 million. @kar2025 split the usual-status female workforce from 2017--18 to 2023--24 into principal-only, subsidiary-only and combined components from the unit-level data, note that close to half of the growth came in the last two years, and find a fall in code 93 and a rise in code 92 with subsidiary self-employment, with a sudden rise in recorded free collection of firewood in three states. They argue that the revised instructions were illustrations rather than new criteria and put the instruction effect at no more than about 2 of the 16.6 percent growth in the rural female workforce in 2023--24, and 1.5 of the 12.4 percent urban growth.

These studies agree that the rise is rural and in self-employment, and they disagree about what it means. @kar2025 already decompose the rise into principal and subsidiary components year by year, and @thakur2025if and @kar2025 trace the movement from code 93 to code 92 with subsidiary self-employment. Their published summaries do not report design-based standard errors for the subsidiary-only share of the full-period rise, and their published summaries do not report a comparison of the rise in persons with the rise in hours per woman, an employment rate consistent with the 2013 international definition estimated from the destination-of-output question, or a shift-share test of composition. These are the elements that distinguish more work from more workers and work for the market from own-use production. The dating of the instruction changes also matters for the measurement explanation: if the clarifications came late in the period, they cannot account for the part of the rise that occurred before them, although they may account for part of what came after.

## Measuring women's work beyond India

The measurement problem is general. In agricultural economies, a large part of women's work is on family farms, in livestock and in collection, often for the household's own use and often combined with domestic work. Plot-level data from six African countries show that women's share of crop labor is substantial and varies with how labor is recorded [@palacios2017]. A survey experiment in Tanzania found that women's measured employment depended on whether a short or detailed questionnaire was used and on whether the woman answered for herself [@bardasi2011]. A survey experiment in Ghana found that farm labor recorded with different recall and respondent designs differed substantially [@gaddis2021]. The ILO's pilot studies for the 2013 standards tested alternative questionnaires in several countries and recommended keeping specific recovery questions on agricultural activity where subsistence or mixed agricultural work is common [@benes2018].

The 2013 standards change what is counted as employment. Production of goods mainly for the household's own final use, such as subsistence farming, kitchen gardens, household poultry and collection of firewood and water, is a form of work but not employment [@ilo2013]. Countries that adopt the standards therefore face two sources of change in the measured employment of women at once: a narrower definition, which lowers it, and more careful probing of agricultural and household activities, which raises recorded work. Distinguishing the two requires exactly the information that the PLFS provides in 2023--24: the capacity in which work is done, hours, and the destination of output. India's experience shows what a headline rate can do when the second source operates without the first.

The conceptual change in the 2013 standards is easy to misread. The resolution does not say that production for the household's own use is not work. It says that such production is work outside the category of employment, and it asks countries to measure employment and own-use production work separately [@ilo2013]. The purpose is to keep an employment indicator that is tied to market participation and income, while making the unpaid productive work of households, which falls disproportionately to women, visible in its own statistics. The PLFS follows the older production boundary of the national accounts, so it counts own-use primary production as economic activity [@nso2016man; @nso2023man]. This is a different concept, not an error. The destination-of-output question brings the two concepts together in one instrument, but it classifies work by purpose and not by activity. The answer depends on the respondent's view of what the household mostly does with its output. That mix can vary across seasons and years, and a household may sell in some periods and consume in others. For this reason the lower and upper bounds should be read as a range that depends on the classification rule, and not as a precise estimate of employment in the international sense. The pilot work that informed the standards stressed that recovering agricultural and subsistence activity requires specific questions [@benes2018], which is the same sensitivity that makes the classification hard.

## Concepts in the PLFS

The PLFS classifies each person by usual activity status over the 365 days preceding the survey. The principal status is the activity on which a person spent a relatively long time. A person whose principal status is outside the labor force, such as domestic duties, is counted as a worker in a subsidiary capacity if she was engaged in an economic activity for at least 30 days in the year. The headline 'usual status (ps+ss)' measure counts both principal and subsidiary workers. Status in employment distinguishes own-account workers and employers, unpaid helpers in household enterprises, regular wage or salaried employees and casual laborers. A separate current weekly status classifies persons by their activity in the seven days before the survey, and the survey records the hours actually worked on each of those days.

India's national definition of economic activity follows the System of National Accounts production boundary. It includes all production of primary goods, including free collection of uncultivated crops, firewood and fish, whether for sale or for the household's own consumption [@nso2016man; @nso2023man]. Two codes for persons outside the labor force are relevant: code 92 (attended domestic duties only) and code 93 (attended domestic duties and was also engaged in free collection of goods, sewing, tailoring or weaving for household use). A woman who does domestic work and also collects firewood or vegetables for the household is therefore recorded either as code 93 or, if the collection amounts to 30 days or more in the year, as a subsidiary own-account worker.

The PLFS continues to use the broader concept of work that preceded the 2013 resolution. In 2023--24, however, the survey asked self-employed persons in primary-sector activities whether their output was for own consumption only, mainly for own consumption, mainly for sale or entirely for sale. This question was not asked in 2017--18.

## Changes in the field instructions

The definitions above are the same in the field instructions for both survey years. The 2023--24 instructions add three elements that the 2017--18 instructions do not contain (Table A1). First, the list of examples of economic activities 'for which special care is needed', which enumerators are told to probe so that such activities are 'not omitted', has a new item: 'Working in kitchen garden, orchards, household poultry, dairy, free collection of fish, small game, wild fruits, vegetables, etc. for household consumption/sale' [@nso2023man]. Second, a new box of worked examples explains how to distinguish codes 92 and 93 from subsidiary self-employment. In one example, a woman whose main activity is domestic duties and who collects firewood for the household for an hour or two a day for at least 30 days in the year is to be recorded with principal status 92 and a subsidiary economic activity as an own-account worker, not as code 93. Third, a further box applies the same logic to the daily activity record of the current weekly status. The survey's note on updated instructions states that the clarifications in the two boxes of worked examples were first provided for the 2022--23 survey; it does not date the new item in the list [@nso2023note]. They clarify rather than change the concepts, but they direct attention to the activities that are most likely to be under-reported among women.

# Data and Methods

## Data

I use the unit-level data of the first visit of PLFS 2017--18 and PLFS 2023--24, released by the National Statistics Office of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. The first-visit schedules cover the rural and urban samples and are the basis of the official annual estimates in usual status. The files contain `r f0(npers(2017))` persons in `r f0(nhh(2017))` households and `r f0(nfsu(2017))` first-stage units in 2017--18, and `r f0(npers(2023))` persons in `r f0(nhh(2023))` households and `r f0(nfsu(2023))` first-stage units in 2023--24. The analysis sample is persons aged 15 and over: `r f0(nwom(2017))` women in 2017--18 (an exact count, `r f0(nw(2017, "Rural"))` rural and `r f0(nw(2017, "Urban"))` urban) and `r f0(nwom(2023))` women in 2023--24, with men used for comparison. The data are anonymized official survey records released for research use; the study involved no contact with participants, and no ethics approval was required for this secondary analysis.

Estimates use the survey multipliers as prescribed in the data documentation: the multiplier is divided by 100 when the sub-sample and the sub-round match and by 200 otherwise, and by the number of quarters to give annual estimates. Standard errors account for the stratified multistage design, with first-stage units within quarter as primary sampling units and the survey strata and sub-strata within state and sector as strata, using the survey package in R [@lumley2004]. Because the two years are independent samples, the standard error of a change is the square root of the sum of the two squared standard errors. I harmonize state codes across years by combining Jammu and Kashmir with Ladakh and Dadra and Nagar Haveli with Daman and Diu, so that both years refer to the same territories.

## Definitions

A person is a usual-status worker if her principal status is a work code (11--51), or if her principal status is not a work code and she reports a subsidiary economic activity with a work code. Workers are classified by the status of the principal activity for principal workers and of the subsidiary activity for subsidiary-only workers, into own-account workers and employers (codes 11--12), unpaid helpers (21), regular wage or salaried employees (31) and casual laborers (41, 51). Agriculture is NIC 2008 divisions 01--03. Weekly hours are the hours actually worked in all economic activities on the seven days before the survey. These are the official definitions, and with them the estimates reproduce the published figures (see Results).

## Measures beyond the headline rate

Three measures complement the headline WPR. The principal-status WPR counts only women whose main activity in the year was economic. Mean weekly hours of work per woman in the population, including zeros for women who did not work, is a measure of the volume of work that is not affected by where the line between workers and non-workers is drawn. For 2023--24, an own-use-adjusted WPR excludes self-employed women in primary-sector activities whose output was for own consumption only or mainly, which approximates the 2013 international definition of employment; excluding only output for own consumption only gives an upper bound, as discussed under Results.

## Decompositions

Because the WPR is the sum of the shares of the population in each status, the change in the WPR is the exact sum of the changes in the status-specific ratios, and the same holds for the split into principal and subsidiary-only workers and into agriculture and other industries. To assess whether the rise reflects changes in the composition of the population, I use a Kitagawa decomposition [@kitagawa1955]. With cells *c* defined by state, rural or urban sector, age group (15--24, 25--34, 35--44, 45--59, 60+), education (below primary, primary or middle, secondary or higher secondary, graduate or above) and marital status, the change in the WPR is

ΔW = Σ~*c*~ *r̄*~*c*~ Δ*p*~*c*~ + Σ~*c*~ *p̄*~*c*~ Δ*r*~*c*~ ,

where *p*~*c*~ is the population share of cell *c*, *r*~*c*~ its WPR, and bars denote averages of the two years. The first term is the composition component and the second the rate component. Cells present in only one year (`r f(k("wpr", "unmatched_pop"), 2)` percent of the population) are excluded from the decomposition and the shares are renormalized.

## Use of AI tools

The author used Claude (Anthropic) to improve the language and readability of parts of the text and to assist with code review and checking. The author reviewed and verified all outputs and takes full responsibility for the content.

# Results

## Reproducing the official estimates

The estimates from the unit-level data reproduce the published figures. For `r nval` published values (the LFPR, WPR and unemployment rate in usual status and the LFPR and WPR in current weekly status, for men and women, in rural areas, urban areas and the whole country, in both years), `r nexact` are identical after rounding to one decimal place and the remaining one (the `r paste0(vlab[vmiss$ind], " for ", tolower(vmiss$sexl), " in ", vmiss$year, "--", substr(vmiss$year + 1, 3, 4))`, published as `r f(vmiss$pub)` and estimated as `r f2(vmiss$est)`) differs by `r f2(abs(vmiss$est - vmiss$pub))` points. Table 1 shows the national values. The women's WPR rose from `r f(w("wpr", "y17"))` to `r f(w("wpr", "y23"))` percent, a rise of `r f(dW)` points (`r ci(dW, w("wpr", "se_d"))`). Men's WPR rose by `r f(m("wpr"))` points, from `r f(m("wpr", "y17"))` to `r f(m("wpr", "y23"))` percent. The women's unemployment rate fell from `r f(urr(2017, "Women"))` to `r f(urr(2023, "Women"))` percent, so almost all of the rise in participation took the form of employment.

```{r tab1, results="asis"}
lab <- c(LFPR = "LFPR, usual status", WPR = "WPR, usual status", UR = "Unemployment rate, usual status", LFPR_CWS = "LFPR, current weekly status", WPR_CWS = "WPR, current weekly status")
T1 <- V[secl == "Total"]
T1 <- dcast(T1, ind + sexl ~ year, value.var = c("pub", "est"))
T1[, ind := factor(ind, levels = names(lab))]; setorder(T1, ind, -sexl)
T1o <- T1[, .(Indicator = lab[as.character(ind)], Sex = sexl, p17 = f(pub_2017), e17 = f(est_2017, 2), p23 = f(pub_2023), e23 = f(est_2023, 2))]
tab(T1o, "**Table 1** Published and reproduced headline estimates, persons aged 15 and over, India (percent)",
    c("Indicator", "Sex", "2017--18 published", "2017--18 estimated", "2023--24 published", "2023--24 estimated"),
    paste0("Published values from the NSO press note of 23 September 2024. Estimated values are computed from the unit-level data with the official weights. ", nexact, " of ", nval, " published values (including rural and urban values not shown) are reproduced exactly after rounding to one decimal place; estimated values are shown to two decimals, so, for example, 68.65 is consistent with a published 68.6 or 68.7, and the one exception is noted in the text."), align = "llrrrr")
```

## Where the rise occurred

Table 2 and Fig. 1 decompose the change in the women's WPR. Nationally, own-account work and employers added `r f(w("s_own"))` points and unpaid helpers `r f(w("s_help"))` points, together `r f0(selfsh)` percent of the rise of `r f(dW)` points. Regular wage employment added `r f(w("s_reg"))` points and casual labor `r f(w("s_cas"))` points. Agriculture accounts for `r f(w("ag"))` points, or `r sh(w("ag"), dW)` percent. The rise in principal workers was `r f(w("ps"))` points; the share of women who are workers only in a subsidiary capacity rose almost five-fold, from `r f(w("ss", "y17"))` to `r f(w("ss", "y23"))` percent, and accounts for `r sh(w("ss"), dW)` percent of the rise.

The rise was concentrated in rural areas. Among rural women the WPR rose by `r f(w("wpr", s = "Rural"))` points, from `r f(w("wpr", "y17", "Rural"))` to `r f(w("wpr", "y23", "Rural"))` percent. Unpaid helpers added `r f(w("s_help", s = "Rural"))` points, of which `r f(w("s_help_ss", s = "Rural"))` points were subsidiary-only helpers, and own-account workers added `r f(w("s_own", s = "Rural"))` points, of which `r f(w("s_own_ss", s = "Rural"))` were subsidiary-only. Subsidiary-only workers account for `r sh(w("ss", s = "Rural"), w("wpr", s = "Rural"))` percent of the rural rise and agriculture for `r sh(w("ag", s = "Rural"), w("wpr", s = "Rural"))` percent. Regular wage employment of rural women rose by `r f(w("s_reg", s = "Rural"))` points, and casual labor in a principal capacity did not change (`r f(w("s_cas_ps", s = "Rural"))` points).

Urban women's WPR rose by a smaller `r f(w("wpr", s = "Urban"))` points, and the composition was different: regular wage employment rose by `r f(w("s_reg", s = "Urban"))` points, own-account work by `r f(w("s_own", s = "Urban"))` points and unpaid help by `r f(w("s_help", s = "Urban"))` points, while casual labor fell slightly. Most of the urban rise was in principal status and outside agriculture.

Men's employment changed in the same direction but on a much smaller scale. Men's WPR rose by `r f(m("wpr"))` points; unpaid help rose by `r f(m("s_help"))` points and subsidiary-only work by `r f(m("ss"))` points, from `r f(m("ss", "y17"))` to `r f(m("ss", "y23"))` percent of men. In proportional terms, however, men's subsidiary-only rate rose nearly as much as women's: it was `r f(m("ss", "y23") / m("ss", "y17"))` times its 2017--18 level in 2023--24, against `r f(w("ss", "y23") / w("ss", "y17"))` times for women (ratios computed from unrounded estimates). The shift toward self-employment and subsidiary work therefore affected both sexes, but for women it was large enough to nearly double the measured employment rate.

```{r tab2, results="asis"}
rows <- c(wpr = "Worker-population ratio", s_own = ind("Own-account worker or employer"), s_help = ind("Unpaid helper"), s_reg = ind("Regular wage or salaried"), s_cas = ind("Casual labor"),
          ps = ind("Principal status"), ss = ind("Subsidiary status only"),
          s_own_ss = ind("Own-account, subsidiary only", 2), s_help_ss = ind("Unpaid helper, subsidiary only", 2),
          ag = ind("Agriculture"), nag = ind("Other industries"))
cell <- function(s, v) { x <- EW[secl == s & var == v]; c(f(x$y17), f(x$y23), paste0(f(x$d), " (", f2(x$se_d), ")")) }
mk <- function(v) as.list(c(rows[[v]], cell("Rural", v), cell("Urban", v), cell("Total", v)))
hdr <- function(t) as.list(c(paste0("*", t, "*"), rep("", 9)))
T2 <- rbindlist(c(list(mk("wpr"), hdr("By status in employment")), lapply(c("s_own", "s_help", "s_reg", "s_cas"), mk),
                  list(hdr("By capacity")), lapply(c("ps", "ss", "s_own_ss", "s_help_ss"), mk),
                  list(hdr("By industry")), lapply(c("ag", "nag"), mk)))
tab(T2, "**Table 2** Decomposition of the women's worker-population ratio by status, capacity and industry, women aged 15 and over (percent of population)",
    c("", "Rural 2017--18", "Rural 2023--24", "Rural change (SE)", "Urban 2017--18", "Urban 2023--24", "Urban change (SE)", "All India 2017--18", "All India 2023--24", "All India change (SE)"),
    paste0("Usual status (ps+ss). Components in each panel sum to the worker-population ratio, up to rounding. The subsidiary-only share of the 2017--18 to 2023--24 change in the WPR is ", f(shs("share")), " percent (SE ", f(shs("se")), "; 95 percent CI ", f(shs("lo")), "--", f(shs("hi")), "), by the delta method with the two rounds treated as independent samples. Agriculture is NIC 2008 divisions 01--03. Standard errors account for the survey design."), align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 9)))
```

```{r fig1, fig.cap = "**Fig. 1** Contributions to the change in women's worker-population ratio, 2017--18 to 2023--24, by status and capacity (percentage points). Bars show point estimates; whiskers show 95 percent confidence intervals", fig.height = 3.6, fig.width = 7.5}
cats <- c(s_own_ps = "Own-account, principal", s_own_ss = "Own-account, subsidiary", s_help_ps = "Helper, principal", s_help_ss = "Helper, subsidiary",
          s_reg_ps = "Regular, principal", s_reg_ss = "Regular, subsidiary", s_cas_ps = "Casual, principal", s_cas_ss = "Casual, subsidiary")
F1 <- EW[var %in% names(cats)][, cat := factor(cats[var], levels = rev(cats))]
F1[, lo := d - 1.96 * se_d][, hi := d + 1.96 * se_d][, secl := factor(secl, levels = c("Rural", "Urban", "Total"), labels = c("Rural", "Urban", "All India"))]
p1 <- ggplot(F1, aes(x = d, y = cat)) + geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.7) + geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, orientation = "y") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) + facet_wrap(~secl, nrow = 1) + labs(x = "Change in percentage points", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
print(p1)
ggsave(file.path(FIGDIR, "Fig1.eps"), p1, device = "eps", width = 7.5, height = 3.6)

## From domestic duties to work

The rise in work was mirrored by a fall in the share of women whose principal activity was domestic duties. Because the two surveys are independent cross-sections, these are net changes in shares, not observed transitions of individual women. Table 3 shows the distribution of women by usual principal activity. Among rural women, the share whose principal activity was domestic duties only (code 92) fell from `r f(pd(2017, "Rural", "Domestic duties only"))` to `r f(pd(2023, "Rural", "Domestic duties only"))` percent, while the share in domestic duties combined with free collection and similar activities for the household (code 93) was almost unchanged (`r f(pd(2017, "Rural", "Domestic duties and free collection"))` and `r f(pd(2023, "Rural", "Domestic duties and free collection"))` percent). Principal-status unpaid helpers rose from `r f(pd(2017, "Rural", "Unpaid helper"))` to `r f(pd(2023, "Rural", "Unpaid helper"))` percent and principal-status own-account workers from `r f(pd(2017, "Rural", "Own-account/employer"))` to `r f(pd(2023, "Rural", "Own-account/employer"))` percent. Together, the principal-status work categories of rural women rose by `r f(w("ps", s = "Rural"))` points, close to the fall in the domestic-duties-only share. The shares in education and in other categories outside the labor force changed little. In urban areas, too, the domestic-duties-only share fell, from `r f(pd(2017, "Urban", "Domestic duties only"))` to `r f(pd(2023, "Urban", "Domestic duties only"))` percent.

The rise in subsidiary-only work took place within the domestic-duties categories, since subsidiary-only workers are, by construction, women whose principal activity is outside the labor force. In 2023--24, `r f(ssp(2023, "Rural", "Domestic duties only"))` percent of rural subsidiary-only women workers had domestic duties only (code 92) as their principal status and `r f(ssp(2023, "Rural", "Domestic duties and free collection"))` percent had code 93, proportions similar to 2017--18. What changed is the number of such women: the subsidiary-only WPR of rural women rose from `r f(w("ss", "y17", "Rural"))` to `r f(w("ss", "y23", "Rural"))` percent. For India as a whole, women in codes 92 and 93 with a subsidiary activity account for `r f0(ddsh)` percent of the rise in the WPR. The rise in women's employment therefore consists to a large extent of women who are still mainly engaged in domestic duties but now report, or are recorded as having, a secondary economic activity.

The distinction between principal and subsidiary status matters for interpretation because the two statuses describe different relations to work. A principal worker spent most of the year in an economic activity. A subsidiary-only worker reports that her main activity was outside the labor force, usually domestic duties, and that she also did some economic work during the year, above a minimum threshold of days. The headline measure adds the two groups, but they are not equivalent. Taken at face value, the rise in subsidiary-only work is not a movement of women out of the home into a job. It is an increase in the number of women who combine domestic duties with some economic activity. Three readings are consistent with that pattern. Women may have started activities that they did not do before. Women who already did such work may have done more of it, so that it crossed the threshold. Or the same activity may have been recorded where it earlier went unrecorded. Each reading has different implications for hours, for earnings and for the reliability of the series, and the data separate them only partly. The porous boundary between domestic and economic activity is a long-standing theme in the literature on time use [@hirway2011; @deshpande2024]. Panel evidence of frequent movement of Indian women into and out of work suggests that many subsidiary workers may be in transitional or intermittent positions [@sarkar2019].

```{r tab3, results="asis"}
ord <- c("Own-account/employer", "Unpaid helper", "Regular wage", "Casual labour", "Unemployed", "In education", "Domestic duties only", "Domestic duties and free collection", "Other not in labour force")
T3 <- dcast(PD, pcat ~ secl + year, value.var = "pct")
T3 <- T3[match(ord, pcat)]
T3o <- T3[, .(Status = c("Own-account worker or employer", "Unpaid helper", "Regular wage or salaried", "Casual labor", "Unemployed", "Attending education", "Domestic duties only (92)", "Domestic duties and free collection etc. (93)", "Other, not in labor force"),
              r17 = f(Rural_2017), r23 = f(Rural_2023), rd = f(Rural_2023 - Rural_2017), u17 = f(Urban_2017), u23 = f(Urban_2023), ud = f(Urban_2023 - Urban_2017))]
tab(T3o, "**Table 3** Women aged 15 and over by usual principal activity status (percent)",
    c("Usual principal activity status", "Rural 2017--18", "Rural 2023--24", "Rural change", "Urban 2017--18", "Urban 2023--24", "Urban change"),
    "Principal status only; women in codes 92, 93, education and other categories may also be subsidiary workers. Columns sum to 100.", align = "lrrrrrr")
```

## Intensity of work

A worker in usual status may have worked very little in any given week. Table 4 reports, for women who are usual-status workers, the share who were employed in the reference week by current weekly status, mean hours actually worked in the week (including zero for those who did not work) and the share who worked fewer than 20 hours. Among all women workers, the share employed in the reference week fell from `r f(iw(2017, "all:Total", "share_cws"))` to `r f(iw(2023, "all:Total", "share_cws"))` percent, mean weekly hours fell from `r f(iw(2017, "all:Total", "hours"))` to `r f(iw(2023, "all:Total", "hours"))`, and the share working fewer than 20 hours rose from `r f(iw(2017, "all:Total", "lt20"))` to `r f(iw(2023, "all:Total", "lt20"))` percent.

Part of the fall in average hours reflects the changed composition of workers. Subsidiary-only workers worked few hours in both years: subsidiary-only helpers averaged `r f(iw(2017, "help:Subsidiary only", "hours"))` hours in 2017--18 and `r f(iw(2023, "help:Subsidiary only", "hours"))` hours in 2023--24, and `r f0(iw(2023, "help:Subsidiary only", "lt20"))` percent of them worked fewer than 20 hours in 2023--24. Their number rose several-fold. Hours also fell within the principal-status groups, by `r f(iw(2017, "help:Principal", "hours") - iw(2023, "help:Principal", "hours"))` hours for principal-status helpers and `r f(iw(2017, "own:Principal", "hours") - iw(2023, "own:Principal", "hours"))` hours for principal own-account workers.

A summary measure that is not affected by where the line between workers and non-workers is drawn is the mean weekly hours of work per woman in the population. Because first visits are spread over all four quarters of the survey year, it averages over seasons, although a single reference week can still miss intermittent work. It rose from `r f2(hs(2017, "hrs"))` (SE `r f(hs(2017, "se.hw"), 3)`) to `r f2(hs(2023, "hrs"))` (SE `r f(hs(2023, "se.hw"), 3)`) hours, an increase of `r hrsg` percent. (Unlike the per-worker means in Table 4, this measure also counts the hours of women employed in the reference week who were not usual-status workers, `r f(R$HDIAG[year == 2017]$pct_cws_not_usual, 2)` percent of women in 2017--18 and `r f(R$HDIAG[year == 2023]$pct_cws_not_usual, 2)` percent in 2023--24.) The WPR rose by `r wprg` percent over the same period. In rural areas, hours per woman rose from `r f2(hp(2017, "Women", "Rural"))` to `r f2(hp(2023, "Women", "Rural"))`, and in urban areas from `r f2(hp(2017, "Women", "Urban"))` to `r f2(hp(2023, "Women", "Urban"))`. One caution is that weekly hours per worker also fell for men, from `r f(iw(2017, "men:Total", "hours"))` to `r f(iw(2023, "men:Total", "hours"))`, and hours per man in the population fell from `r f2(hp(2017, "Men"))` to `r f2(hp(2023, "Men"))`. Part of the fall in hours per worker may therefore reflect changes in how hours were reported rather than changes specific to women; if so, the increase in hours per woman may be understated. Even so, the rise in women's hours of work is about half the rise in the share of women counted as workers.

```{r tab4, results="asis"}
g4 <- c("all:Total" = "All women workers", "all:Rural" = ind("Rural"), "all:Urban" = ind("Urban"),
        "own:Principal" = "Own-account, principal", "own:Subsidiary only" = "Own-account, subsidiary only",
        "help:Principal" = "Unpaid helper, principal", "help:Subsidiary only" = "Unpaid helper, subsidiary only",
        "reg:Principal" = "Regular wage, principal", "cas:Principal" = "Casual labor, principal", "cas:Subsidiary only" = "Casual labor, subsidiary only",
        "men:Total" = "All men workers (comparison)")
T4 <- rbindlist(lapply(names(g4), function(g) as.list(c(g4[[g]], f(iw(2017, g, "share_cws")), f(iw(2023, g, "share_cws")), f(iw(2017, g, "hours")), f(iw(2023, g, "hours")), f(iw(2017, g, "lt20")), f(iw(2023, g, "lt20"))))))
tab(T4, "**Table 4** Intensity of work among usual-status workers aged 15 and over",
    c("", "Employed in reference week (%) 2017--18", "Employed in reference week (%) 2023--24", "Mean hours worked in week 2017--18", "Mean hours worked in week 2023--24", "Worked under 20 hours (%) 2017--18", "Worked under 20 hours (%) 2023--24"),
    paste0("Hours actually worked in all economic activities in the seven days before the survey, including zero for workers who did not work in that week. Regular wage workers in a subsidiary capacity only are few and not shown. Means are over usual-status workers. Hours per woman in the text also count women employed in the reference week who are not usual-status workers (", f(R$HDIAG[year == 2017]$pct_cws_not_usual, 2), " percent of women in 2017--18 and ", f(R$HDIAG[year == 2023]$pct_cws_not_usual, 2), " percent in 2023--24), so hours per woman divided by the WPR slightly exceeds the 2017--18 means shown here."), align = "lrrrrrr")
```

## Production for the household's own use

The 2023--24 survey asked self-employed persons in primary-sector activities (NIC divisions 01--09) about the destination of their output. Among women own-account workers and helpers in these activities, `r f(et("Women", 1))` percent reported that the output was for own consumption only, `r f(et("Women", 2))` percent that it was mainly for own consumption with some sale, `r f(et("Women", 3))` percent that it was mainly for sale and `r f(et("Women", 4))` percent that it was entirely for sale (Table 5). The corresponding share for own consumption only or mainly was `r f(et("Men", 1) + et("Men", 2))` percent among men. `r if (max(R$ECOcov$miss) < 0.05) "The question was answered for all of these workers." else paste0("The answer is missing for ", f(R$ECOcov[sexl == 'Women']$miss), " percent of these women workers (weighted).")` Production mainly for own use was most common among rural women working in a subsidiary capacity: `r f(ec("Women", "Rural", "Subsidiary only", 1:2))` percent of them produced only or mainly for the household, compared with `r f(ec("Women", "Rural", "Principal", 1:2))` percent of rural women working in a principal capacity.

Under the 2013 international definition, production of goods intended mainly for the household's own final use is own-use production work, not employment [@ilo2013]. Table 5 shows how the 2023--24 WPR would change if such work were excluded. Excluding women whose output was for own consumption only lowers the women's WPR from `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr"))` to `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x1"))` percent; also excluding those whose output was mainly for own consumption lowers it to `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x12"))` percent. For rural women, the corresponding values are `r f(ou("Women", "Rural", "wpr"))`, `r f(ou("Women", "Rural", "wpr_x1"))` and `r f(ou("Women", "Rural", "wpr_x12"))` percent. These are approximations: the classification is by destination of output and applies only to self-employment in primary activities, and some excluded women may have other work that the survey does not record. They also cannot be compared with 2017--18, when the question was not asked. They show, however, that a substantial part of measured employment of women in 2023--24 is production mainly for the household, which the 2013 standard classifies as own-use production work rather than employment.

```{r tab5, results="asis"}
eco_lab <- c("Own consumption only", "Mainly own consumption, some sale", "Mainly for sale", "Entirely for sale")
d5 <- function(sx, s, cp) sapply(1:4, function(e) f(ec(sx, s, cp, e)))
T5a <- data.table(Destination = eco_lab, wrp = d5("Women", "Rural", "Principal"), wrs = d5("Women", "Rural", "Subsidiary only"),
                  wa = sapply(1:4, function(e) f(et("Women", e))), ma = sapply(1:4, function(e) f(et("Men", e))))
T5b <- data.table(Destination = c("WPR as published definition", "Excluding own consumption only", "Excluding own consumption only or mainly"),
                  wrp = c(f(ou("Women", "Rural", "wpr")), f(ou("Women", "Rural", "wpr_x1")), f(ou("Women", "Rural", "wpr_x12"))),
                  wrs = c(f(ou("Women", "Urban", "wpr")), f(ou("Women", "Urban", "wpr_x1")), f(ou("Women", "Urban", "wpr_x12"))),
                  wa = c(f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr")), f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x1")), f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x12"))),
                  ma = c(f(ou("Men", "Total", "wpr")), f(ou("Men", "Total", "wpr_x1")), f(ou("Men", "Total", "wpr_x12"))))
T5 <- rbind(T5a,
            data.table(Destination = "*Panel B: WPR, 2023--24*", wrp = "*Women, rural*", wrs = "*Women, urban*", wa = "*Women, all*", ma = "*Men, all*"), T5b)
tab(T5, "**Table 5** Destination of output of self-employed workers in primary activities, and the worker-population ratio excluding production for own use, 2023--24 (percent)",
    c("Panel A: destination of output", "Women, rural, principal", "Women, rural, subsidiary only", "Women, all", "Men, all"),
    "Column headings for Panel B are given in its first row. Panel A: own-account workers, employers and unpaid helpers in NIC 2008 divisions 01--09, by capacity in which the activity is pursued; columns sum to 100. Panel B: worker-population ratio of persons aged 15 and over, after excluding self-employed workers in these divisions whose output was for own consumption only, or only or mainly. Each person is classified by the activity that makes her a worker: the principal activity if it is work, otherwise the subsidiary activity; a woman whose principal activity is wage work is not excluded even if she also farms for own use. The question was not asked in 2017--18.", align = "lrrrr")
```

## Composition

Women's employment varies strongly with age, education, marital status and place of residence, so part of the change in the WPR could reflect changes in the composition of the population between the two surveys. Table 6 shows that it does not. With `r f0(k("wpr", "ncell"))` cells defined by state, sector, age group, education and marital status, the composition component is `r f(k("wpr", "composition"), 2)` points and the rate component is `r f(k("wpr", "rates"), 2)` points. Composition slightly lowered the expected ratios of casual labor and unpaid help and slightly raised that of regular wage employment. The composition component is between `r f(min(K2$composition), 2)` and `r f(max(K2$composition), 2)` points for all sets of cells considered, including cells that add social group (Table A2, Panel A). Restricting the population to women of working age (15--59) gives the same picture: their WPR rose by `r f(r15("wpr"))` points, of which `r f(r15("ss"))` points were subsidiary-only work (Table A2, Panel B). The rise in women's employment took place within groups of women, not through a shift toward groups with higher employment.

```{r tab6, results="asis"}
kl <- c(wpr = "Worker-population ratio", s_own = ind("Own-account worker or employer"), s_help = ind("Unpaid helper"), s_reg = ind("Regular wage or salaried"), s_cas = ind("Casual labor"))
T6 <- K[, .(Component = kl[var], total = f(total, 2), composition = f(composition, 2), rates = f(rates, 2))]
tab(T6, "**Table 6** Kitagawa decomposition of the change in women's worker-population ratio, 2017--18 to 2023--24 (percentage points)",
    c("", "Total change", "Composition", "Rates within cells"),
    paste0("Cells: state by sector by age group by education by marital status (", f0(k("wpr", "ncell")), " cells present in both years). Women aged 15 and over."), align = "lrrr")
```

## Who and where

The rise was broad-based but uneven (Table 7). Among rural women, the WPR rose by `r f(het("agegrp", "15-24"))` points for those aged 15--24 and by `r f(het("agegrp", "35-44"))` and `r f(het("agegrp", "45-59"))` points for those aged 35--44 and 45--59. It rose more for women with below-primary (`r f(het("edu4", "Below primary"))` points) or primary or middle schooling (`r f(het("edu4", "Primary or middle"))` points) than for graduates (`r f(het("edu4", "Graduate or above"))` points). It rose in every quintile of household consumption per person, least in the poorest (`r f(het("mpceq", "1"))` points) and by `r f(het("mpceq", "3"))` and `r f(het("mpceq", "5"))` points in the middle and richest quintiles. It rose most among Scheduled Tribe women, from `r f(het("socl", "Scheduled Tribe", col = "2017"))` to `r f(het("socl", "Scheduled Tribe", col = "2023"))` percent. Among the youngest rural women, the rise came mostly through subsidiary work (`r f(het("agegrp", "15-24", v = "ss"))` of `r f(het("agegrp", "15-24"))` points). In urban areas the increases were smaller in every group.

```{r tab7, results="asis"}
glab <- c(agegrp = "Age group", edu4 = "Education", mpceq = "Household consumption quintile", socl = "Social group")
lv <- list(agegrp = c("15-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-59", "60+"), edu4 = c("Below primary", "Primary or middle", "Secondary or higher secondary", "Graduate or above"),
           mpceq = as.character(1:5), socl = c("Scheduled Tribe", "Scheduled Caste", "Other Backward Class", "Others"))
T7 <- rbindlist(lapply(names(lv), function(g) rbindlist(c(list(list(Group = paste0("*", glab[[g]], "*"), r17 = "", r23 = "", rd = "", u17 = "", u23 = "", ud = "")), lapply(lv[[g]], function(l) {
  r <- H[group == g & level == l & variable == "wpr"]
  lab <- if (g == "mpceq") c("Q1 (poorest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5 (richest)")[as.integer(l)] else gsub("-", "--", l)
  list(Group = ind(lab), r17 = f(r[secl == "Rural"][["2017"]]), r23 = f(r[secl == "Rural"][["2023"]]), rd = f(r[secl == "Rural"]$d),
       u17 = f(r[secl == "Urban"][["2017"]]), u23 = f(r[secl == "Urban"][["2023"]]), ud = f(r[secl == "Urban"]$d)) })))))
tab(T7, "**Table 7** Women's worker-population ratio by group, women aged 15 and over (percent)",
    c("", "Rural 2017--18", "Rural 2023--24", "Rural change", "Urban 2017--18", "Urban 2023--24", "Urban change"),
    "Usual status (ps+ss). Consumption quintiles are of monthly household consumption expenditure per person, within year and sector.", align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Across the `r nrow(B)` most populous states, the change in women's WPR ranged from `r f(bg("Andhra Pradesh"))` points in Andhra Pradesh and `r f(bg("Delhi"))` points in Delhi to `r f(bg("Jharkhand"))` points in Jharkhand and `r f(bg("Assam"))` points in Assam (Fig. 2; Table A3 gives the state values). Across these states, the correlation between the change in the WPR and the change in the combined ratio of own-account workers and helpers is `r f2(R$st_cor)`. States differed in which of the two categories rose: in Jharkhand, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh it was mainly unpaid helpers, in Assam and West Bengal mainly own-account workers. Because self-employment accounts for most of the national rise, this correlation is partly mechanical. The exceptions are states with smaller rises in which wage work accounted for half or more of the change, such as Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Delhi (Table A3). Elsewhere the pattern of a rise concentrated in self-employment holds, so the national result does not reflect a few states with unusual estimates.

```{r fig2, fig.cap = "**Fig. 2** Change in women's worker-population ratio and in the self-employed (own-account plus helper) ratio, 20 most populous states, 2017--18 to 2023--24 (percentage points). Marker area is proportional to population; the dashed line marks equal changes", fig.height = 4.2, fig.width = 6.2}

F2 <- merge(F2, lab, by = "name", all.x = TRUE)
F2[is.na(side), `:=`(side = "R", dy = 0)]
F2[, lx := se + ifelse(side == "R", 0.8, -0.8)][, ly := wpr + dy][, hj := ifelse(side == "R", 0, 1)][, lead := abs(dy) >= 1][, lname := gsub(" & ", " and ", name, fixed = TRUE)]
p2 <- ggplot(F2, aes(x = se, y = wpr)) + geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) + geom_point(aes(size = pop / 1e6), shape = 21, fill = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(data = F2[lead == TRUE], aes(x = se, y = wpr, xend = lx, yend = ly), linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey40") +

# Discussion and Conclusion

The accounting establishes five facts about the measured rise in Indian women's employment between 2017--18 and 2023--24. It was a rise in self-employment, mostly in agriculture and mostly in rural areas. Nearly half of it consisted of women whose principal activity was outside the labor force, mostly domestic duties (`r f0(ddsh)` percent of the rise is in the two domestic-duties codes), and who were counted as workers through a subsidiary activity. It amounted to a much smaller increase in hours of work than in the number of workers. And a large share of the self-employment of women in primary production in 2023--24 was production mainly for the household's own consumption. And changes in population composition do not account for the rise.

## Competing interpretations

These facts are consistent with more than one interpretation, and the data cannot separate them. If more women took up or expanded work on family farms and livestock because of pressure on household incomes, the rise would look like this [@apu2023; @jha2026]. If additional family labor reflects productive opportunities in agriculture and allied activities, the pattern would also look like this [@goldar2026]. And if the same activities were recorded more completely, after field instructions that direct enumerators to probe for kitchen gardens, poultry, dairy and free collection and explain when such activity makes a woman engaged in domestic duties a subsidiary worker, the rise would again look like this [@thakur2025]. The categories that rose are the ones most sensitive to probing in the measurement literature [@langsten2008; @bardasi2011; @gaddis2021]: unpaid family work, subsidiary activity, small-scale livestock and collection, and production for own use.

Some patterns bear on the relative importance of these explanations without settling it. The worked examples in the instructions describe women who would otherwise be coded 93 being recorded instead with principal status 92 and a subsidiary activity; such a reclassification would, other things equal, lower the share in code 93. That share hardly changed among rural women and rose among urban women, while the share in code 92 fell, mainly because more women reported a principal economic activity. These endpoint shares cannot show a reclassification confined to one year: the year-on-year counts show a fall in code 93 and a rise in code 92 with subsidiary self-employment between 2022--23 and 2023--24 [@thakur2025if; @kar2025], and @kar2025 bound the resulting effect at about 2 of the 16.6 percent growth in the rural female workforce in that year (1.5 of 12.4 percent in urban areas). The rise was also gradual: in the published series, the women's WPR was 22.0, 23.3, 28.7, 31.4, 31.7, 35.9 and 40.3 percent in the seven years from 2017--18 to 2023--24 [@nso2024pn], so about half of the rise (`r f0(halfsh)` percent) had occurred by 2021--22, before the worked examples that the survey's note dates to 2022--23. The pace then accelerated, from about `r f(pace1)` points a year between 2017--18 and 2021--22 to about `r f(pace2)` points a year between 2021--22 and 2023--24, and the acceleration coincides with the clarifications. The timing therefore cuts both ways. An explanation that rests only on the 2023--24 instructions cannot account for the part of the rise that came before them, and the undated new item in the list of activities needing special care may have been introduced earlier; but the faster rise afterwards is consistent with an effect of the instructions, which the published series cannot separate from post-pandemic recovery or other changes in the same years. These patterns are suggestive rather than diagnostic. And men also show a rise in unpaid help and subsidiary work, on a smaller scale. The annual unit-level analysis of @kar2025 addresses the timing directly; what it cannot provide, and what a full assessment would need, is an experimental comparison of probing versions within the survey.

Several threats to comparability across the two rounds deserve explicit mention, apart from the change in instructions. The first is seasonality and the reference period. The usual-status measure covers a full year, so it depends on recall, and the weekly measure depends on the week of the interview. Both can respond differently to changes in the share of the year that women spend in agricultural tasks. The second is the identity of the respondent. Survey experiments show that whether a woman answers for herself or another household member answers for her affects measured employment [@bardasi2011]. A change in the practice of who is interviewed would therefore change the series without any change in behavior. The third is the quality of enumeration and supervision. Experimental evidence shows that the design of recall questions changes recorded farm labor [@gaddis2021], and the field note on updated instructions shows that guidance evolved between rounds [@nso2023note]. The fourth is the sampling frame and the design weights; if the frame represents some groups of households better in one round than in the other, levels can shift without any change in within-group rates. The fifth is the economic setting. The period includes a pandemic and its aftermath, and household enterprises and agricultural work may have absorbed labor for reasons unrelated to survey procedure. None of these threats can be assessed with two cross-sections alone, and none should be treated as established. They indicate what a fuller test of comparability would need.

## What the headline rate does and does not mean for policy

Whatever the mix of causes, the findings have implications for how the rise is used. Measured as hours, the increase in women's work is about half as large as measured by the WPR. Excluding production mainly for the household's own use, the rule closest to the 2013 international definition of employment, the women's WPR in 2023--24 would be `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x12"))` percent rather than `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr"))` percent; excluding only output used solely by the household gives an upper bound of `r f(ou("Women", "Total", "wpr_x1"))` percent. Both figures keep the 365-day usual-status basis of the PLFS rather than the short reference period of the 2013 standards, so they approximate rather than reproduce the international measure. Comparisons of India's women's employment with other countries, or with earlier Indian estimates, should therefore use comparable measures: hours, principal status, or employment excluding own-use production.

The headline rate is often used as a summary of women's economic participation, in national assessments and in international comparisons. The results suggest what it does and does not tell users. It does tell them that many more women are recorded as doing some economic activity in the year, and that this is true within groups of women defined by age, education, marital status, sector and state. It does not by itself tell them that women's paid employment, earnings or hours of market work rose in proportion. Regular wage employment accounts for `r sh(w("s_reg"), dW)` percent of the rise; unpaid help, which by definition brings no direct individual income, accounts for `r sh(w("s_help"), dW)` percent; and a large part of the self-employment of women in primary production is mainly for the household's own consumption. Programs whose objectives concern women's earnings, social-security coverage or access to wage work are better monitored with measures of paid employment and earnings than with the headline rate. Programs concerned with the time burden on women, such as those providing water, fuel or childcare, are better monitored with hours of work and time use, because the activities that rose (collection, kitchen gardens, livestock) compete with domestic work for women's time. And targets expressed as a women's participation or employment rate are best accompanied by the principal-status rate and an hours-based measure, so that progress toward them can be read correctly.

The PLFS already contains the information needed to produce such measures. Publishing them alongside the headline rates, and reporting principal and subsidiary workers separately, would make the series easier to interpret without new data collection. The same applies to the destination-of-output question: tabulating the employment rate with and without production mainly for own use would let users compare India's figures with those of countries that have adopted the 2013 standards.

The same point applies to international gender monitoring. Global frameworks, including the Sustainable Development Goal indicators on gender equality and decent work, rely on a small set of measures that national statistical offices report: employment and participation rates, the share of employment that is informal, the time spent on unpaid domestic and care work, and wage or earnings gaps. A rise in a women's employment rate is normally read in these frameworks as progress. The Indian case shows that the rate alone can be a poor guide when the rise lies in unpaid or own-use forms of work. Indicators that count the same activity both as employment and as unpaid work would send contradictory signals, and cross-country rankings would depend on whether a country has adopted the 2013 definitions [@ilo2013]. A practical response is to report, for each country, a core set of linked indicators: the employment rate under the 2013 definition, the rate under the broader national concept, the principal-status rate, and hours. Countries that keep the broader concept, as India does, could report the destination-of-output tabulation as a bridge. Such reporting does not judge any national choice. It allows users to see which concept underlies a figure before they compare it, and it reduces the risk that a measurement change is read as a change in women's economic position.

## Lessons for surveys elsewhere

The Indian case also carries lessons for other countries whose labor force surveys are moving to the 2013 standards. First, where a large share of women's work is in agriculture, livestock and collection, the measured employment rate of women can change substantially with changes in probing, even when definitions are fixed; survey experiments have shown this within a single survey [@bardasi2011; @gaddis2021; @benes2018], and the PLFS shows it is compatible with a large movement in a national series. Second, separating principal from subsidiary activity, and persons from hours, provides an internal check on whether a rise in the employment rate reflects more work or more workers. Third, a single question on the destination of output allows a survey to report both the older, broader concept of work and an employment rate consistent with the new standards, which eases the transition between concepts. Fourth, changes to field instructions are part of the measurement system; dating and publishing them, and where possible testing them experimentally, would make it easier to separate changes in women's work from changes in how it is recorded.

## Limitations and conclusion

The analysis has limitations. It compares two years six years apart, and the period includes the COVID-19 pandemic; the end points do not show the path. The decomposition is an accounting, not a causal analysis. The destination-of-output question is available only for 2023--24, so the own-use adjustment cannot be applied to 2017--18. The fall in reported hours for men suggests that hours may not be fully comparable between the years. And the assessment of changes in field instructions is based on the published instructions; the data cannot show how they were applied.

Several kinds of additional data would do more than a third cross-section to settle what the rise means. The first is annual unit-level analysis that extends the year-by-year splits of @kar2025 to hours and to the destination of output, so that each jump can be compared with documented changes in instructions. The second is a split-sample experiment inside the survey, in which a random part of the sample is interviewed with the older instructions and the rest with the current ones. Experiments of this kind have been used elsewhere to measure the effect of questionnaire design on women's recorded work [@bardasi2011; @gaddis2021], and they are the cleanest way to separate recording from behavior. The third is longitudinal information on the same women, which would show whether subsidiary workers remain in that status, move to principal work or return to domestic duties. The fourth is linked time-use data, which would show how the added work is distributed over the day and how it relates to domestic work [@hirway2011]. The fifth is plot-level or enterprise-level information on household farms, which has been valuable in other settings for understanding who supplies labor to which tasks [@palacios2017]. Process information on interviews, such as the respondent and the interview length, would also help. Together, these sources would let future work move from an accounting of the rise to a test of its causes [@thakur2025].

The rise in women's employment in India between 2017--18 and 2023--24 is reproduced, to within rounding, by the unit-level data, and it is real in the sense that the survey records many more women as workers under formally unchanged definitions, although the guidance to enumerators changed. It is concentrated in own-account work and unpaid help in agriculture, in rural areas, among women whose principal activity is outside the labor force, mostly domestic duties, and in production often mainly for the household's own use. It is not explained by changes in the composition of the population, and in hours of work it is about half as large. The rise therefore lies largely in forms of work close to the boundary of what surveys count as work. Whether it reflects new work, more work by women already working, or more complete recording of existing work matters for how it is read, and answering that question will require the measures this paper proposes to be tracked over time, in India and in other countries where much of women's work lies near that boundary.
